66	
67	## HTTP API
68	
69	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
70	
71	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
72	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
73	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
74	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
75	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
76	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
77	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
78	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
79	
80	### Tenants and quotas
81	
82	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
83	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
84	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
85	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
86	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
87	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
88	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
89	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
90	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
91	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
92	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
93	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
94	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
95	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
96	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
97	
98	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
99	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
100	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, queue pulls, acknowledgements,
101	and all history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics
102	queries. An empty
103	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
104	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
105	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
106	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
107	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
108	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
109	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
110	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
111	the usual `409 conflict`.
112	
113	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
114	hold:
115	
116	```http
117	PUT /quotas
118	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
119	X-Tenant-Id: acme
120	
121	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
122	```
123	
124	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
125	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
126	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
127	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
128	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
129	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
130	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
131	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
132	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
133	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
134	
135	```http
136	GET /quotas
137	X-Tenant-Id: acme
138	```
139	
140	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
141	when the tenant has declared none.
142	
143	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
144	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
145	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
146	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
147	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
148	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
149	
150	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
151	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
152	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
153	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
154	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
155	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
156	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
157	
158	### Usage metering and billing
159	
160	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
161	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
162	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
163	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
164	metered action types are:
165	
166	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
167	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
168	  definition;
169	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
170	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
171	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
172	  `schedule_triggered`;
173	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
174	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
175	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
176	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
177	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
178	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
179	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
180	  meters nothing.
181	
182	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
183	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
184	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
185	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
186	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
187	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
188	
189	```http
190	GET /usage
191	X-Tenant-Id: acme
192	```
193	
194	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
195	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
196	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
197	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
198	
199	```http
200	GET /bill
201	X-Tenant-Id: acme
202	```
203	
204	Returns the per-type bill:
205	
206	```json
207	{"bill":{"items":[
208	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
209	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
210	],"total":2100}}
211	```
212	
213	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
214	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
215	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
216	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
217	
218	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
219	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
220	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
221	
222	### Operational metrics
223	
224	```http
225	GET /metrics
226	X-Tenant-Id: acme
227	```
228	
229	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
230	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
231	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
232	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
233	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
234	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
235	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
236	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
237	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
238	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
239	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
240	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
241	
242	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
243	timestamp ending in `Z`:
244	
245	```http
246	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
247	X-Tenant-Id: acme
248	```
249	
250	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
251	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
252	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
253	  counts every recorded fact;
254	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
255	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
256	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
257	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
258	  result.
259	
260	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
261	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
262	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
263	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
264	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
265	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
266	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
267	completion or termination event.
268	
269	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
270	
271	```http
272	GET /metrics/export
273	X-Tenant-Id: acme
274	```
275	
276	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
277	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
278	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
279	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
280	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
281	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
282	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
283	
284	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
285	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
286	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
287	ordered by ascending label value:
288	
289	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
290	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
291	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
292	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
293	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
294	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
295	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
296	  unlabeled scalar samples.
297	
298	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
299	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
300	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
301	ends with a single newline.
302	
303	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
304	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
305	failures, and schedule triggers:
306	
307	```json
308	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
309	```
310	
311	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
312	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
313	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
314	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
315	  ended for that reason.
316	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
317	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
318	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
319	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
320	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
321	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
322	  another attempt, per node identifier.
323	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
324	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
325	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
326	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
327	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
328	
329	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
330	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
331	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
332	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
333	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
334	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
335	
336	### Health
337	
338	```http
339	GET /health
340	```
341	
342	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
343	
344	### Create a workflow
345	
346	```http
347	POST /workflows
348	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
349	
350	{
351	  "id": "order-flow",
352	  "nodes": [
353	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
354	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
355	  ]
356	}
357	```
358	
359	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
360	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
361	
362	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
363	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
364	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
365	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
366	
367	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
368	
369	```json
370	{
371	  "id": "order-flow",
372	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
373	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
374	}
375	```
376	
377	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
378	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
379	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
380	
381	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
382	
383	```json
384	{
385	  "id": "nightly-orders",
386	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
387	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
388	}
389	```
390	
391	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
392	
393	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
394	
395	```json
396	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
397	```
398	
399	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
400	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
401	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
402	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
403	`false`.
404	
405	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
406	
407	```json
408	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
409	```
410	
411	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
412	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
413	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
414	dependencies of its successors.
415	
416	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
417	
418	```json
419	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
420	```
421	
422	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
423	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
424	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
425	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
426	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
427	`retries_exhausted`.
428	
429	A task may instead declare an approval point:
430	
431	```json
432	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
433	```
434	
435	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
436	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
437	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
438	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
439	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
440	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
441	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
442	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
443	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
444	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
445	move the task.
446	
447	### Submit an approval decision
448	
449	```http
450	POST /executions/run-1/decision
451	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
452	
453	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
454	```
455	
456	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
457	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
458	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
459	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
460	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
461	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
462	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
463	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
464	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
465	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
466	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
467	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
468	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
469	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
470	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
471	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
472	404.
473	
474	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
475	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
476	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
477	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
478	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
479	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
480	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
481	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
482	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
483	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
484	shape and event stream.
485	
486	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
487	segment:
488	
489	```json
490	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
491	```
492	
493	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
494	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
495	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
496	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
497	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
498	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
499	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
500	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
501	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
502	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
503	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
504	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
505	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
506	loop node instead).
507	
508	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
509	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
510	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
511	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
512	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
513	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
514	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
515	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
516	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
517	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
518	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
519	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
520	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
521	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
522	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
523	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
524	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
525	belong only to their iterations.
526	
527	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
528	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
529	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
530	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
531	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
532	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
533	exactly.
534	
535	### Dynamic map nodes
536	
537	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
538	recorded array:
539	
540	```json
541	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
542	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
543	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
544	```
545	
546	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
547	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
548	
549	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
550	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
551	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
552	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
553	  the same path syntax as a condition.
554	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
555	  expand.
556	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
557	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
558	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
559	  uses. The template id must not collide with any declared node id and map
560	  template ids must be unique; it only names the dynamically expanded
561	  instances. A map node must not sit inside a loop body, and a loop body must
562	  not contain a map node.
563	
564	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
565	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
566	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
567	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
568	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
569	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
570	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
571	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
572	overwrite another instance.
573	
574	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
575	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
576	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
577	become available in the usual way.
578	
579	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
580	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
581	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
582	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
583	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
584	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
585	
586	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
587	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per instance
588	giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or `failed`),
589	its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a permanently failed
590	instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and the node's single
591	`failure_reason`. The `maps` field is present only when the bound workflow
592	declares a map node; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
593	
594	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
595	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
596	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
597	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
598	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
599	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
600	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
601	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
602	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
603	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
604	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
605	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
606	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
607	other node event.
608	
609	### Workflow versions
610	
611	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
612	
613	```json
614	{
615	  "id": "order-flow",
616	  "version": "2026-09-25",
617	  "nodes": [
618	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
619	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
620	  ]
621	}
622	```
623	
624	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
625	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
626	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
627	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
628	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
629	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
630	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
631	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
632	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
633	
634	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
635	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
636	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
637	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
638	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
639	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
640	
641	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
642	current version at the moment it starts:
643	
644	```http
645	POST /executions
646	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
647	
648	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
649	```
650	
651	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
652	
653	```json
654	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
655	```
656	
657	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
658	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
659	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
660	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
661	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
662	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
663	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
664	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
665	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
666	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
667	conclusions never change.
668	
669	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
670	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
671	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
672	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
673	stream with no added field.
674	
675	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
676	
677	```http
678	GET /workflows/order-flow
679	```
680	
681	```json
682	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
683	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
684	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
685	]}
686	```
687	
688	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
689	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
690	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
691	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
692	resources as usual.
693	
694	### Migrate a running execution to another version
695	
696	```http
697	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
698	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
699	
700	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
701	```
702	
703	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
704	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
705	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
706	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
707	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
708	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
709	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
710	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
711	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
712	carries the target version.
713	
714	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
715	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
716	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
717	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
718	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
719	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
720	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
721	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
722	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
723	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
724	
725	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
726	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
727	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
728	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
729	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
730	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
731	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
732	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
733	content.
734	
735	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
736	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
737	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
738	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
739	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
740	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
741	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
742	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
743	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
744	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
745	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
746	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
747	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
748	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
749	
750	### Start an execution
751	
752	```http
753	POST /executions
754	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
755	
756	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
757	```
758	
759	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
760	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
761	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
762	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
763	
764	An execution may declare a timeout:
765	
766	```json
767	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
768	```
769	
770	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
771	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
772	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
773	a timeout never expire.
774	
775	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
776	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
777	
778	```json
779	{
780	  "id": "run-3",
781	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
782	  "input": {},
783	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
784	}
785	```
786	
787	### Inspect an execution
788	
789	```http
790	GET /executions/run-1
791	GET /executions/run-1/events
792	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
793	```
794	
795	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
796	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
797	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
798	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
799	
800	### Webhook notifications
801	
802	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
803	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
804	
805	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
806	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
807	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
808	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
809	  reason);
810	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
811	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
812	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
813	
814	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
815	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
816	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
817	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
818	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
819	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
820	subscriptions" below.
821	
822	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
823	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
824	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
825	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
826	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
827	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
828	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
829	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
830	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
831	triggered it.
832	
833	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
834	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
835	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
836	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
837	results as before.
838	
839	### Inspect the delivery history
840	
841	```http
842	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
843	```
844	
845	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
846	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
847	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
848	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
849	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
850	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
851	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
852	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
853	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
854	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
855	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
856	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
857	
858	### Queue subscriptions
859	
860	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
861	
862	```json
863	{
864	  "id": "run-4",
865	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
866	  "input": {},
867	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
868	}
869	```
870	
871	A queue subscription contains exactly:
872	
873	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of at most 100 characters;
874	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
875	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
876	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
877	
878	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
879	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
880	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
881	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
882	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
883	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
884	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
885	
886	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
887	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
888	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
889	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
890	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
891	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
892	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
893	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
894	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
895	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
896	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
897	before.
898	
899	### Inspect the queue state
900	
901	```http
902	GET /executions/run-4/queues
903	X-Tenant-Id: acme
904	```
905	
906	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
907	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
908	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
909	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
910	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
911	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
912	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
913	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
914	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
915	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
916	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
917	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
918	
919	### Pull messages from a queue
920	
921	```http
922	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
923	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
924	X-Tenant-Id: acme
925	
926	{}
927	```
928	
929	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
930	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
931	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
932	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
933	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
934	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
935	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
936	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
937	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
938	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
939	
940	### Acknowledge a message
941	
942	```http
943	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
944	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1
945	X-Tenant-Id: acme
946	
947	{"idempotency_key": "run-4:2:queue:order-events"}
948	```
949	
950	The body must contain exactly `idempotency_key`, naming a message of the
951	queue. Acknowledgement is explicit and final: the message permanently leaves
952	the queue and is never delivered again, and the response is
953	`{"acknowledged": true}`. Acknowledging a message that was already
954	acknowledged, or a key the queue does not know, is a 404 `not_found`.
955	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one
956	belonging to a missing or cross-tenant execution, is likewise a 404
957	`not_found`. Pull and acknowledge are idempotent commands like every other
958	operation: repeating one with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the
959	original result, and reusing a key across different operations is a 409
960	`conflict`.
961	
962	### Schedules
963	
964	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
965	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
966	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
967	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
968	
969	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
970	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
971	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
972	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
973	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
974	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
975	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
976	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
977	
978	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
979	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
980	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
981	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
982	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
983	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
984	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
985	created is exposed through the status query below.
986	
987	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
988	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
989	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
990	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
991	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
992	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
993	
994	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
995	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
996	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
997	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
998	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
999	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
1000	
1001	### Declare or replace a schedule
1002	
1003	```http
1004	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1005	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
1006	
1007	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
1008	```
1009	
1010	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
1011	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
1012	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
1013	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
1014	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
1015	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
1016	
1017	### Inspect the schedule status
1018	
1019	```http
1020	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1021	```
1022	
1023	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
1024	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
1025	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
1026	
1027	```json
1028	{
1029	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
1030	  "paused": false,
1031	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
1032	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
1033	}
1034	```
1035	
1036	The fields are:
1037	
1038	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
1039	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
1040	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
1041	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
1042	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
1043	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
1044	  `null` until the first period fires;
1045	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
1046	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
1047	
1048	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
1049	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
1050	
1051	### Pause and resume a schedule
1052	
1053	```http
1054	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
1055	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
1056	
1057	{}
1058	```
1059	
1060	```http
1061	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
1062	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
1063	
1064	{}
1065	```
1066	
1067	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
1068	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
1069	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
1070	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
1071	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
1072	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
1073	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
1074	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
1075	
1076	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
1077	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
1078	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
1079	
1080	### Checkpoints
1081	
1082	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
1083	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
1084	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
1085	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
1086	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
1087	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
1088	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
1089	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
1090	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
1091	duplicating any node output.
1092	
1093	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
1094	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
1095	same state shape and event stream as before.
1096	
1097	### Complete the next ready node
1098	
1099	```http
1100	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1101	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
1102	
1103	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
1104	```
1105	
1106	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
1107	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
1108	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
1109	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
1110	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
1111	the status becomes `completed`.
1112	
1113	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
1114	
1115	```http
1116	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1117	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
1118	
1119	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
1120	```
1121	
1122	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
1123	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
1124	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
1125	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
1126	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
1127	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
1128	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
1129	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
1130	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
1131	
1132	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
1133	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
1134	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
1135	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
1136	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
1137	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
1138	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
1139	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
1140	the execution stream.
1141	
1142	### Cancel an execution
1143	
1144	```http
1145	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
1146	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
1147	```
1148	
1149	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
1150	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
1151	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
1152	
1153	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
1154	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
1155	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
1156	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
1157	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
1158	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
1159	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
1160	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
1161	
1162	### Claim a work item
1163	
1164	```http
1165	POST /executions/run-1/claim
1166	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
1167	
1168	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
1169	```
1170	
1171	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
1172	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
1173	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
1174	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
1175	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
1176	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
1177	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
1178	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
1179	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
1180	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
1181	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
1182	
1183	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
1184	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
1185	
1186	```http
1187	POST /executions/run-1/advance
1188	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
1189	
1190	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1191	```
1192	
1193	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
1194	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
1195	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
1196	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
1197	an execution without any claim.
1198	
1199	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
1200	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
1201	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
1202	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
1203	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
1204	
1205	### Renew a lease
1206	
1207	```http
1208	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
1209	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
1210	
1211	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1212	```
1213	
1214	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
1215	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
1216	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
1217	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
1218	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
1219	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
1220	
1221	### Release a work item
1222	
1223	```http
1224	POST /executions/run-1/release
1225	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
1226	
1227	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
1228	```
1229	
1230	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
1231	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
1232	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
1233	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
1234	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
1235	`not_found`.
1236	
1237	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
1238	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
1239	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
1240	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
1241	restarts.
1242	
1243	### Recover from a checkpoint
1244	
1245	```http
1246	POST /executions/run-1/recover
1247	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
1248	
1249	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
1250	```
1251	
1252	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
1253	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
1254	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
1255	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
1256	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
1257	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
1258	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
1259	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
1260	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
1261	execution state and events.
1262	
1263	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
1264	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
1265	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
1266	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
1267	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
1268	stays consistent with the materialized state.
1269	
1270	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
1271	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
1272	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
1273	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
1274	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
1275	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
1276	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
1277	
1278	### Replay
1279	
1280	```http
1281	POST /executions/run-1/replay
1282	```
1283	
1284	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
1285	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
1286	and the rebuilt execution.
1287	
1288	## Errors
1289	
1290	Errors use this shape:
1291	
1292	```json
1293	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
1294	```
1295	
1296	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
1297	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
1298	declarations and the usage, bill, and metrics queries require a tenant, and
1299	quota limits are positive integers validated by the
1300	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
1301	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
1302	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
1303	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
1304	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
1305	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
1306	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
1307	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
1308	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
1309	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
1310	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
1311	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
1312	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
1313	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
1314	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
1315	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
1316	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
1317	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
1318	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1319	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, more than ten attempts, a
1320	subscription declaring both `url` and `queue` or neither, an empty queue
1321	name, or a non-positive visibility timeout — is a
1322	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
1323	querying the delivery history or the queues of a missing execution is a
1324	missing resource. Declaring a queue name another workflow or execution of
1325	the same tenant already declared is a conflict. Pulling from or
1326	acknowledging a missing queue, and acknowledging an unknown or already
1327	acknowledged message, are missing resources; a pull body that is not an
1328	empty object, or an acknowledgement body without exactly an
1329	`idempotency_key` string, is a validation error. An approval
1330	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
1331	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
1332	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
1333	A map node with an unknown or missing field, a mistyped or non-positive
1334	`max_instances`, an invalid or colliding template, a `source` that is not a
1335	task dependency, an invalid `path`, or a map node inside a loop body (or a
1336	loop body containing a map) is likewise a validation error that rejects the
1337	whole request.
1338	A decision by an approver who is
1339	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
1340	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
1341	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
1342	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
1343	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
1344	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
1345	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
1346	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
1347	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
1348	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
1349	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
1350	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
1351	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
1352	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
1353	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
1354	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
1355	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
1356	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
1357	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
1358	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
1359	
1360	## Tests
1361	
1362	```bash
1363	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
1364	```
1365	
1366
